source_citation: Caesar, De Bello Gallico I; Wikipedia 'Battle of Bibracte'
notes: Caesar's demographic/casualty claims (368000 migrants; 238000 enemy dead) are rejected by most modern historians as self-serving inflation; figures here use Delbrueck-range modern estimates instead of Caesar's own tally.

source_citation: Caesar, De Bello Gallico II; Livius.org 'Battle of the Sabis'; Wikipedia 'Battle of the Sabis'
notes: Caesar admits his army was nearly overrun by a surprise ambush before rallying. His claim that Nervii fighting strength fell from 60000 to 500 survivors is treated skeptically by modern historians; enemy casualties here use a lower modern estimate.

source_citation: Caesar, De Bello Gallico VII; Wikipedia 'Battle of Gergovia'; historyofwar.org 'Siege of Gergovia'
notes: Caesar's own report to the Senate (46 centurions + ~700 legionaries killed) is widely considered a lowball given the scale of disorder his own narrative describes; own_casualties here is a higher modern estimate. A real repulse, not an army-breaking rout, so decisiveness is left blank per schema convention.

source_citation: Caesar, De Bello Gallico VII; Wikipedia 'Battle of Alesia'
notes: enemy_troop_strength combines the ~80000-strong besieged garrison and a relief army of comparable modern-estimated size (~80000), engaged near-simultaneously during the climactic double battle; Caesar's own relief-army figure of 250000 is the single most commonly cited example of Caesarian troop-count exaggeration.

source_citation: Caesar, De Bello Civili I; Wikipedia 'Battle of Ilerda'
notes: A maneuver campaign rather than a pitched battle; won largely bloodlessly by cutting supply lines, which secured all of Hispania. Joint Pompeian command (Afranius and Petreius); Afranius recorded as the primary of the two.

source_citation: Caesar, De Bello Civili III; Wikipedia 'Battle of Dyrrhachium (48 BC)'
notes: Pompey broke Caesar's blockade and inflicted a real defeat but failed to press the advantage; Caesar's army retreated intact rather than breaking, so decisiveness is left blank rather than marked Rout.

source_citation: Caesar, De Bello Civili III; Appian, Civil Wars II; Wikipedia 'Battle of Pharsalus'
notes: enemy_casualties combines ~15000 killed and ~24000 captured. Caesar's claim of only ~200 own casualties is one of the most widely doubted figures in his corpus given the battle's scale; own_casualties here is a modern multiple of that figure.

source_citation: Suetonius; Wikipedia 'Battle of Zela (47 BC)'; historyofwar.org 'Battle of Zela'
notes: Source of the 'veni, vidi, vici' quote; a 5-day campaign. Casualty figures are thinly documented in the ancient sources -- among the least quantified battles in this dataset.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Ruspina'; historyofwar.org 'Battle of Ruspina'
notes: A near-disaster for a newly-landed, poorly-supplied force caught in the open by Numidian cavalry under Labienus; extricated rather than routed, with no lasting strategic effect. Casualty figures are anecdotal ('as much as a third of the force') rather than a hard ancient tally -- among the softest-sourced rows in this dataset.

source_citation: Bellum Africum (ancient, not by Caesar); Wikipedia 'Battle of Thapsus'; Britannica 'Battle of Thapsus'
notes: Ancient accounts describe Caesar's own troops going out of control during the collapse, killing beyond his orders; the ancient figure of ~50 own casualties is almost certainly propagandistic and is treated as a floor, not a real count.

source_citation: Bellum Hispaniense (ancient, not by Caesar); Wikipedia 'Battle of Munda'; History Hit 'Battle of Munda'
notes: Nominal Pompeian command was nineteen-year-old Gnaeus Pompeius the Younger, but Titus Labienus held tactical field command, so he is recorded as opponent_general_id. Called Caesar's bloodiest battle by total field carnage, though his own losses were comparatively light; the tradition that Caesar considered suicide mid-battle is treated as color, not a quantifiable data point.

source_citation: Arrian Anabasis I; Diodorus Siculus XVII; Wikipedia 'Battle of the Granicus'
notes: Persian troop strength is contested: Arrian gives ~40,000 (slightly more than Alexander's own force), other ancient breakdowns imply ~35,000; modern historians treat these as roughly comparable in scale rather than picking one figure. enemy_casualties combines an estimated ~4,000 Persian cavalry/infantry killed in the actual fighting with ~9,000 of the 18,000 Greek mercenaries in Persian service who were surrounded and killed after the Persian collapse -- a much-noted atrocity since they had offered surrender.

source_citation: Arrian Anabasis I; Diodorus Siculus XVII; Wikipedia 'Siege of Halicarnassus'; Warfare History Network 'A Storm of Terrors: Alexander the Great at Halicarnassus'
notes: One of the softer-sourced rows in this dataset: ancient accounts name only ~40 notable Macedonian dead (including three named officers), not a full army count; own_casualties here is a rough order-of-magnitude estimate for a multi-week siege with several assaults and surprise sorties, not a directly attested total. Memnon burned the city and withdrew by sea with part of the garrison once the walls fell, so resistance continued from the citadel after Alexander took the city proper -- objective_secured is still true for the city itself.

source_citation: Arrian Anabasis II; Curtius Rufus III; Wikipedia 'Battle of Issus'
notes: Darius's army size is one of the widest-ranging figures in ancient historiography: ancient sources claim 300,000-600,000, modern estimates run anywhere from 25,000 to 100,000; 60,000 is used here as a mid-range modern estimate, not a consensus figure. own_casualties combines Curtius's reported 450 killed and 4,500 wounded, which matches the modern estimate of 'just below 5,000' total Macedonian casualties.

source_citation: Arrian Anabasis II; Curtius Rufus IV; Wikipedia 'Siege of Tyre (332 BC)'
notes: Tyre's pre-siege population was ~40,000 but most non-combatants were evacuated to Carthage before the siege closed; enemy_troop_strength here is an estimate of the remaining fighting garrison, not the city's population. enemy_casualties follows Curtius's count of ~6,000 fighting men killed in the final storm plus ~2,000 crucified afterward, close to Arrian's alternative figure of 8,000 killed overall (the two ancient accounts disagree on the breakdown, not the rough scale). No single Tyrian field commander is identifiable -- King Azemilcus was away serving with the Persian fleet during the siege -- so opponent_general_id is left blank per schema convention. Alexander's king of Cyprus and defecting Phoenician crews supplied most of the 223 ships used; own_troop_strength reflects the land army, since naval crews aren't separately tracked in this schema.

source_citation: Arrian Anabasis II; Curtius Rufus IV; Wikipedia 'Siege of Gaza (332 BC)'
notes: own_casualties of 10,000 (22% of the besieging force) is the figure given by the commonly cited secondary sources, but no primary-source breakdown for it was found in this pass, and it is unusually high for a fortress with a 15,000-man garrison; flagged here rather than silently accepted or silently 'corrected' to a number with no citation behind it. Alexander himself was wounded (shoulder) during the siege, which took three failed assaults and 100 days before falling -- consistent with a real and costly fight even if the precise figure is uncertain. decisiveness is marked Pyrrhic given the casualty ratio, not Strategic, despite the campaign-level payoff (it opened the road to Egypt).

source_citation: Arrian Anabasis III; Diodorus Siculus XVII; Wikipedia 'Battle of Gaugamela'
notes: Persian troop strength is the most extreme example of ancient exaggeration in this dataset: ancient sources claim 250,000-1,000,000, modern logistics-based estimates (e.g. Engels, Marsden) run 50,000-250,000; 100,000 is used here as a mid-range modern estimate. enemy_casualties of ~50,000 is likewise mid-range against a modern estimate spread of 40,000-90,000; Arrian's claim of 300,000+ captured is not used. This battle effectively ended the Achaemenid Empire as a field-army power, hence Strategic despite Darius himself escaping.

source_citation: Arrian Anabasis IV; Wikipedia 'Siege of Cyropolis'
notes: One of the thinnest-sourced rows in this dataset: the Wikipedia summary itself flags reliance on a single primary source, and ancient accounts disagree on whether the city surrendered (Ptolemy's version) or was stormed with its inhabitants massacred (Aristobulus's version); the stormed version is used here since it is the one with a casualty figure attached. own_casualties is a rough 'light-to-moderate' estimate (no hard ancient figure survives) informed by Alexander and Craterus both being wounded during the fighting. No single defending commander is named in the sources, so opponent_general_id is left blank. Part of the wider Sogdian revolt that Jaxartes (fought the same season) also responds to.

source_citation: Arrian Anabasis IV; Wikipedia 'Battle of Jaxartes'
notes: enemy (Saka/Scythian) troop strength is not given by ancient sources at all; 20,000 here is a rough estimate consistent with the scale of a raiding force able to threaten Alexander's Jaxartes frontier, not a cited ancient figure -- among the least quantified rows in this dataset. own_casualties combines the reported 160 killed and ~1,000 wounded. Repelled a Scythian incursion during the Sogdian revolt but did not end the revolt itself (Spitamenes remained at large), hence Tactical rather than Strategic.

source_citation: Arrian Anabasis V; Diodorus Siculus XVII; Wikipedia 'Battle of the Hydaspes'
notes: Porus's army size is disputed even among modern historians (30,000-54,000); 50,000 used here as within the commonly-cited range. enemy_casualties follows Arrian's ~20,000 infantry killed rather than Diodorus's lower 12,000-killed/9,000-captured breakdown. Tactically the most difficult fight of the campaign (rain-soaked ground, 200 war elephants) and its aftermath -- the army's refusal to march further east at the Hyphasis days later -- is sometimes read as making this a Pyrrhic turning point for the campaign as a whole rather than a clean Strategic win; Strategic is used here since the battle itself was decisively won and the mutiny is a separate event not captured by a single battle row.

source_citation: Secret History of the Mongols; Osprey 'Mongol Warrior 1200-1350'; Wikipedia 'Battle of Chakirmaut'
notes: Sources disagree on Temujin's own troop count: 66,000 (attributed to Osprey's 'Mongol Warrior 1200-1350') vs. 80,000 (cited in some secondary summaries referencing Richard Gabriel's 'Genghis Khan's Greatest General'); 66,000 is used here since it pairs consistently with an 80,000-strong Naiman-led coalition in the narrative of Temujin being significantly outnumbered before Jamukha's defection tipped the battle. No source, primary or modern, gives a specific casualty count for either side -- only that Temujin's losses were 'low' and the coalition's 'heavy', with survivors reportedly falling to their deaths fleeing along Mount Naqu's cliffs. own_casualties and enemy_casualties here are order-of-magnitude estimates consistent with that qualitative language, not source-given figures; this is among the softest-sourced rows in this general's dataset. Jamukha, nominal coalition leader, defected mid-battle; Tayang Khan (killed in the fighting) is recorded as opponent_general_id as the Naiman king around whom the coalition was actually built.

source_citation: Yuan Shi (via secondary summaries); Warfare History Network 'The Mongol Hordes Invade China'; Wikipedia 'Mongol conquest of Western Xia'
notes: Troop strength (75,000 Mongol vs. 150,000 Western Xia) follows Warfare History Network's summary of the campaign; no primary breakdown was independently verified. The siege ended in a negotiated Xia surrender and tribute (including a Xia princess given in marriage) rather than a storming of the city, so casualties are likely to have been comparatively low relative to the sieges of the later Khwarazmian campaign -- but no source quantifies them beyond a single concrete anecdote: Genghis's attempt to flood the city by diverting the Yellow River backfired and swept away 'hundreds' of his own troops instead, which is the only hard anchor for own_casualties in this row (the figure above should be read as reflecting that flood disaster specifically, not a full accounting of eight months of siege losses, and is almost certainly an undercount). enemy_casualties has no source anchor at all and is an order-of-magnitude placeholder consistent with a siege that ended in negotiation rather than sack. No single Xia field commander distinct from Emperor Li Anquan (Xiangzong), who personally negotiated the surrender, is identifiable, so opponent_general_id is left blank. decisiveness is Strategic rather than Rout since Western Xia continued to exist as a Mongol vassal after this campaign; it was not conquered outright until 1227.

source_citation: Paul Ratchnevsky, Genghis Khan: His Life and Legacy; Wikipedia 'Battle of Yehuling'
notes: Troop figures follow historian Paul Ratchnevsky's estimate (65,000 Mongol soldiers plus 10,000 allied troops, combined here as own_troop_strength); Jin strength is one of the widest divergences in this dataset -- chronicled totals run 400,000-600,000+ for the whole Jin military establishment, but modern secondary sources estimate the force actually engaged at Yehuling at 30,000-50,000; the modern mid-range estimate is used here rather than the chronicle total, the same approach used for Alexander's Gaugamela row elsewhere in this dataset. Casualties are described only qualitatively in every source found: Mongol losses 'light'/'minimal', the Jin army 'destroyed'/'wiped out' with corpses reportedly covering the retreat route for 'over a hundred miles'. No source gives a specific number for either side; own_casualties and enemy_casualties here are order-of-magnitude estimates consistent with that language, not source-given counts. Multiple Jin commanders are named in the sources (Wanyan Chengyu nominally senior, Hushahu blamed by some accounts for a battlefield collapse) with no clear consensus on a single field commander, so opponent_general_id is left blank.

source_citation: Ata-Malik Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahangushay; Carl Sverdrup, The Mongol Conquests; Wikipedia 'Otrar Catastrophe'
notes: Troop strength uses the mid-range of modern estimates on both sides (50,000-75,000 Mongol; 5,000-15,000 Khwarazmian garrison under Inalchuq); a pro-Mongol chronicler's claim of a 20,000-60,000-strong garrison is treated as inflated and not used, consistent with this dataset's general skepticism toward chroniclers writing for the victors. The five-month siege ended when a Khwarazmian sub-commander (Qaracha) defected and opened the gates; sources describe the Mongols then 'slaughtering most of' the unprepared garrison, which anchors enemy_casualties as a large majority of the garrison estimate. own_casualties has no comparable anchor -- sources describe Mongol losses only as 'minimal' -- and is an order-of-magnitude estimate consistent with that language, not a source-given figure. Inalchuq himself held out afterward in the inner citadel with the remnants of his troops for roughly another month before being captured and executed; recorded here as opponent_general_id since he was both the garrison commander and the officer whose seizure of a Mongol trade caravan triggered the entire Khwarazmian war.

source_citation: Ata-Malik Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahangushay; Carl Sverdrup, The Mongol Conquests; Wikipedia 'Siege of Bukhara'
notes: Troop strength estimates disagree substantially: the commonly cited modern range for the Mongol force is 30,000-50,000, but Carl Sverdrup argues Mongol tuman strength is routinely overstated in secondary literature and gives a higher floor (75,000+); the more commonly cited 30,000-50,000 range (midpoint used here) is kept as the primary figure, with Sverdrup's alternative flagged rather than substituted since it is the outlier position. The defending garrison is even more disputed -- Juvaini's chronicle claims at least 20,000, Sverdrup argues for as few as 2,000-5,000, roughly a tenfold spread; a conservative mid-estimate is used here rather than either extreme. Sources describe the Mongols as killing 'most of the garrison' and 'everybody in the citadel' after a short siege and a failed defenders' sortie, anchoring enemy_casualties as a large majority of the garrison estimate. No source of any kind -- primary or modern, qualitative or numeric -- describes Mongol losses at Bukhara; even infobox-level summaries list Mongol casualties simply as 'Unknown' rather than characterizing them at all. own_casualties here is consequently among the most speculative figures in this general's dataset: a placeholder order-of-magnitude estimate reflecting the near-bloodless character generally attributed to this campaign by modern historians, not any source specific to this battle. No individual Khwarazmian field commander distinct from the 'Gur-Khan' title given in some sources is clearly identifiable, so opponent_general_id is left blank.

source_citation: Ata-Malik Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahangushay; Carl Sverdrup, The Mongol Conquests; Wikipedia 'Siege of Samarkand (1220)'
notes: Defender troop strength is contested even at the order-of-magnitude level: some sources describe 30,000 Qangli regulars plus up to 100,000 local levies, while Sverdrup argues the real garrison was closer to 10,000 given the city's total population of under 100,000; a mid-range modern estimate is used here. enemy_casualties combines Juvaini's account of a roughly 50,000-strong sortie force drawn out and destroyed in the open field (all but an estimated 2,000 survivors), several thousand executed after the citadel's fall, and about a thousand killed repelling an earlier sortie; Juvaini's separate claim of 2,500,000 total killed is explicitly rejected here as impossible on demographic grounds (modern estimates put the entire Khwarazmian Empire's population near 3,000,000) and is not used. As with Bukhara, no source found -- of any kind -- quantifies or even qualitatively characterizes Mongol losses at Samarkand; own_casualties is an order-of-magnitude placeholder, not a source-derived figure, and should be read with the same skepticism as Bukhara's. Shah Muhammad II had already fled before the siege closed, and no single defending field commander among the officers named in the sources (Alp Er Khan, Taghday Khan) is clearly primary, so opponent_general_id is left blank.

source_citation: Ata-Malik Juvayni, Tarikh-i Jahangushay; Minhaj-i-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri; Wikipedia 'Battle of the Indus'
notes: Troop strength for Jalal al-Din's army combines the cited breakdown (3,000 cavalry, 700 bodyguards, 30,000-35,000 semi-irregular troops); this was already a reduced force, since a large portion of his roughly 65,000-strong army at Ghazni deserted (mostly Afghan contingents, over a dispute about spoils) after the earlier Battle of Parwan and before reaching the Indus. enemy_casualties follows the commonly cited figure of 'almost the entire army, 30,000+ killed', with only a small remnant (reportedly around 4,000) reaching the far bank; this matches Genghis's decisive flanking maneuver (a 10,000-man detachment sent around the mountain) collapsing Jalal al-Din's position from two directions. No source found quantifies or characterizes Mongol losses at all; own_casualties is an order-of-magnitude placeholder like Bukhara and Samarkand's, not source-derived. objective_secured is marked false despite the battlefield victory: Genghis's actual aim was to eliminate Jalal al-Din, the last major Khwarazmian claimant, and he escaped by swimming the Indus, going on to contest Mongol rule in Persia and the Caucasus for another decade.

battle_name: Battle of the Yellow River (Lingzhou campaign)
source_citation: EBSCO Research Starters 'Battle of Yellow River'; Wikipedia 'Mongol conquest of Western Xia'
notes: The clearest single account found for this final campaign gives round figures of 180,000 Mongol troops against a Western Xia army of roughly 300,000 positioned along the frozen Yellow River near Lingzhou; these figures come from a single tertiary summary rather than a named primary or academic source independently verified in this research pass, and should be treated with more caution than the Khwarazmian-campaign rows above. Sources describe the Xia army as 'virtually annihilated', anchoring enemy_casualties as a large majority of the engaged force; no source quantifies or characterizes Mongol losses at all, so own_casualties is an order-of-magnitude placeholder consistent with the rest of this dataset's softest rows. This was Genghis's last personally commanded major battle: he died in August 1227 during the ensuing siege of the Xia capital, which fell only after his death and is not included as a separate row since he did not live to see or direct its fall. No individual Tangut field commander is named in the sources found; opponent_general_id is left blank.

battle_name: Battle of the Horns of Hama
source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of the Horns of Hama'; HistoryOfWar.org 'Battle of the Horns of Hamah, 13 April 1175'
notes: Saladin's first major independent-command engagement after Nur ad-Din's death, against a Zengid coalition contesting his move into Syria. Both sides are given as roughly 10,000 each (~20,000 total engaged) with no finer breakdown found. Sources describe the engagement as 'nearly-bloodless' and 'minimal' casualties on both sides despite the numbers involved -- Gokboeri's right wing broke Saladin's left flank before being routed by a charge from Saladin's own guard, and the battle was decided more by the psychological shock of arriving Egyptian reinforcements than by actual fighting. own_casualties and enemy_casualties here are order-of-magnitude estimates consistent with that qualitative language (enemy_casualties set somewhat higher to reflect the final rout of Gokboeri's wing), not source-given counts. opponent_general_id is Muzaffar ad-Din Gokboeri, the Zengid field commander at Hama in 1175 -- notably the same Gokboeri who later defected to Saladin's camp and commanded a wing of his own army at Hattin in 1187.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Montgisard'
notes: The only defeat in pitched battle Saladin suffered before Richard the Lionheart's Third Crusade. Wikipedia's infobox gives Saladin's force as ~26,000 (William of Tyre) against a Crusader force of ~4,500 (80 Templars, 375 other knights, 2,500-4,000 infantry/archers, midpoint used here); the article flags Latin estimates of Saladin's numbers as 'greatly exaggerated' by some modern scholarship, so this figure should be read with real uncertainty. own_casualties is derived from the source's description that Saladin fled to Cairo 'with only a tenth of his army' -- i.e. ~90% losses on a 26,000-strong force -- rather than a direct source-given casualty count. enemy_casualties (1,100 killed, 750 wounded) is the more precisely sourced figure. decisiveness is Rout since Saladin's own army was the one that broke and was largely destroyed, per the schema's definition for a Loss.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Hattin'
notes: The decisive battle of Saladin's career and arguably of the Crusades. Troop-strength sources disagree substantially: the Crusader field army is given as 18,000-20,000 (20,000 used, close to the summed unit breakdown of ~19,700); the Ayyubid force is given as a much wider 20,000-40,000, with the midpoint (30,000) used here rather than either extreme. Muslim losses are described only as 'light, mostly spearmen and some archers' with no source-given count -- own_casualties is an order-of-magnitude placeholder consistent with that language, the same approach used for several Genghis Khan rows elsewhere in this dataset. Crusader losses are near-total: 'the majority of the army captured or killed', with only ~200 knights escaping the field; enemy_casualties (18,000) reflects that near-annihilation against the ~20,000-strong Crusader force, treating captures and enslavements alongside deaths as the schema's 'killed, wounded, captured, and missing' definition requires. decisiveness is Rout: the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem's field army and military capability were destroyed outright, directly opening the way to Jerusalem's fall two months later.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Siege of Jerusalem (1187)'; TheCollector.com 'How Saladin Defeated the Crusaders & Recaptured Jerusalem'
notes: Saladin's besieging army is put at ~20,000; the city's defenders at 'maybe 5,000', a figure the source itself hedges, against a city otherwise 'full of refugees but had few soldiers' -- Balian of Ibelin knighted 'sixty new knights from the ranks of the squires and burgesses' to bolster an initial garrison of under fourteen knights. The siege ended in a negotiated surrender after eight days rather than a storming, so hard combat-casualty figures for either side are essentially unattested; own_casualties and enemy_casualties here are order-of-magnitude placeholders for the mining/sortie fighting that did occur before the surrender, not source-given counts. The commonly-cited figure of 11,000-15,000 Christian civilians enslaved or ransomed after the surrender is a captivity/ransom outcome, not a battle casualty, and is deliberately not used in either casualty field.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Siege of Tyre (1187)'
notes: Saladin's only major failure of the otherwise triumphant 1187 campaign, and historically significant precisely because Tyre's survival gave the Third Crusade a coastal foothold to land at. own_troop_strength uses the midpoint of a 20,000-25,000 range; the '40,000+' Crusader figure almost certainly reflects reinforcements accumulated by sea across the roughly two-month siege rather than a single simultaneous garrison, the same caveat that applies to the Siege of Acre row. Casualties are described only qualitatively (Ayyubid 'heavy', Crusader 'light'), with no source-given count for either side; own_casualties and enemy_casualties are order-of-magnitude placeholders consistent with that language. Saladin personally commanded throughout and made the final call, after consulting his emirs, to disband the siege and withdraw to Acre. decisiveness is left blank per the schema's Loss convention -- a real defeat, but not one where Saladin's own army broke.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Siege of Acre (1189-1191)'
notes: A near two-year siege-within-a-siege: Guy of Lusignan's Crusader army besieged the Ayyubid garrison inside Acre while Saladin's field army in turn encamped outside and besieged the besiegers, unable to break through to relieve the city. As with Caesar's Alesia elsewhere in this dataset, one row combines the whole engagement rather than splitting garrison from relief force: own_troop_strength (45,000) is the midpoint of Saladin's cited 40,000-50,000 relief army; enemy_troop_strength (25,000) is the Crusader army's size by the siege's end, after growing from an initial 7,000-10,000 (total Crusader manpower rotated through the siege over two years is cited as high as 59,000). Some contemporary sources claim Ayyubid losses 'up to 60,000' -- rejected here as implausible on the same grounds Juvaini's inflated Samarkand death toll is rejected elsewhere in this dataset -- with a more conservative order-of-magnitude estimate (15,000, combining garrison and relief-force losses over the full two years) used instead. enemy_casualties (19,000 dead) is a more specific, separately-cited figure; some sources put total Crusader casualties (dead, wounded, and disease losses over two years) as high as 100,000, but the more conservative dead-only figure is used here for consistency with what's actually counted on the Ayyubid side. Guy of Lusignan began and nominally led the siege throughout; Philip II and Richard I arrived only for its final weeks in 1191, so Guy is recorded as opponent_general_id.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Arsuf'
notes: Saladin's repeated attempts to break Richard I's disciplined marching column down the coast to Jaffa failed, and his own harassing cavalry took the worse of the exchange. The source itself cautions that 'losses are difficult to assess with any precision': Christian chronicles claim 32 emirs and 7,000 Ayyubid dead, but the same source notes the true figure 'may have been fewer' -- a more conservative modern-plausible estimate (5,000) is used here rather than the chronicle total, the same treatment given to other chronicle-sourced worst-case figures elsewhere in this dataset (e.g. Samarkand, Acre above). Crusader losses ('no more than 700') are the more specific figure. decisiveness is left blank per the schema's Loss convention: a real tactical defeat that cost Saladin the coast road, but not a case of his own army routing.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Jaffa (1192)'
notes: Saladin's last major action of the Third Crusade and the direct trigger for the September 1192 Treaty of Jaffa truce; he died the following March. Precise day-level dating is skipped (month-only) since the source describes the engagement as extending from a surprise assault on 27 July to a pitched battle on 8 August 1192 without a single clean 'battle date'. own_troop_strength (7,000 cavalry) and enemy_troop_strength (55-80 knights plus ~2,000 infantry, ~2,040 used) both come from the same infobox. own_casualties (700 dead) is the more specific figure; enemy_casualties is a small order-of-magnitude placeholder since the only hard number given is 'at least 2 dead, many wounded' -- an unquantified 'many wounded' with no total. The source separately notes 1,500 Ayyubid horses lost, not counted here since the schema's casualty fields are about troops, not mounts. The source itself flags medieval casualty figures generally as unreliable. decisiveness is left blank per the schema's Loss convention.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Mollwitz'; Christopher Duffy, 'The Army of Frederick the Great'
notes: Frederick's first battle, opening the First Silesian War. Cavalry-heavy Prussian left wing collapsed early and Frederick himself left the field on the advice of his generals, believing the battle lost; the Prussian infantry under Schwerin held and won it in his absence -- a fact widely reported by contemporaries and not glossed over here despite the Win being credited to him as commanding general of record. Troop strength and casualty figures vary by a few thousand across sources (Prussian strength is given anywhere from 16,000 to 23,000); the widely-cited Wikipedia infobox midpoint figures are used.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Chotusitz'
notes: Decisive engagement of the First Silesian War; the Prussian victory directly produced the June 1742 Treaty of Berlin ceding Silesia to Prussia, so objective_secured is true at the campaign level even though Frederick's own cavalry was initially routed and the infantry/artillery carried the win, echoing the pattern at Mollwitz the year before.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Hohenfriedberg'; Duffy, 'Frederick the Great: A Military Life'
notes: Widely regarded by historians (Duffy included) as Frederick's tactical masterpiece of the Second Silesian War -- a night march and dawn assault that crushed a larger Austro-Saxon army attempting to invade Silesia. enemy_casualties (13,700) is the Austro-Saxon killed-and-wounded-plus-captured total commonly cited; a narrower killed/wounded-only reading of the same sources would put it closer to 9,000, so this figure should be read as the inclusive definition the schema calls for (killed, wounded, captured, and missing).

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Soor'
notes: Frederick's army, retreating from Bohemia and outnumbered nearly two to one, was surprised at dawn by Prince Charles of Lorraine's force but rallied and won a defensive battle. Classed Tactical rather than Strategic: it preserved the army and the retreat but did not by itself end the Second Silesian War the way Chotusitz ended the First (that took until the December 1745 Treaty of Dresden, after Kesselsdorf -- a battle excluded from this roster since it was fought and won by Leopold I of Anhalt-Dessau, not Frederick personally, per the same personal-command bar used for Genghis Khan and Saladin elsewhere in this dataset).

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Lobositz'
notes: Opening battle of the Seven Years' War. Tactically muddled and inconclusive in the fighting itself -- casualties were roughly even and some contemporary accounts called it a draw -- but Browne's Austrian army withdrew afterward, leaving Frederick free to complete the blockade that forced the Saxon army's surrender at Pirna two weeks later; objective_secured is true on that campaign-level reading, with the ambiguity of the battle itself noted rather than smoothed over.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Prague (1757)'
notes: One of the bloodliest battles of the war for its size, with roughly proportional casualties on both sides (Prussian Field Marshal Schwerin was killed in the attack). Prague's outcome is Win and objective_secured is true at the immediate level -- the Austrian field army was driven into the city and besieged -- but the follow-on siege was abandoned six weeks later after the defeat at Kolin, so this battle's tactical win did not convert into the campaign win it looked set to produce; that failure belongs to the Kolin row, not this one.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Kolin'
notes: Frederick's first major defeat, and a strategic disaster out of proportion to the tactical margin: a premature and piecemeal Prussian assault on Daun's entrenched relief army failed with heavy losses, forcing Frederick to abandon the six-week siege of Prague and evacuate Bohemia entirely. decisiveness is left blank per the schema's convention (a Loss only takes 'Rout' when the general's own army broke, and the Prussian army retreated in reasonably good order here, unlike at Kunersdorf two years later).

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Rossbach'
notes: Frederick's most celebrated victory: a combined Franco-Imperial army under Soubise and Saxe-Hildburghausen, nearly twice the Prussian strength, was routed in barely 90 minutes of fighting for the loss of only a few hundred Prussians. enemy_casualties (10,000) combines killed/wounded (roughly 3,000) with captured (roughly 5,000-7,000, sources vary); this inclusive reading matches the schema's 'killed, wounded, captured, and missing' definition rather than the smaller killed/wounded-only figure sometimes quoted.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Leuthen'
notes: A month after Rossbach, Frederick used the oblique-order attack against a numerically superior Austrian army defending Silesia after its earlier loss of Breslau, breaking it and recapturing Silesia within weeks. enemy_casualties (22,000) is roughly 10,000 killed/wounded plus 12,000 captured, per the widely-cited totals; frequently named alongside Rossbach as the pair of victories that historians (Napoleon among them, per later commentary) cite as Frederick's clearest demonstrations of tactical genius.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Zorndorf'
notes: Extremely costly and confused fighting against a Russian army under Fermor that had been ravaging Brandenburg; both sides suffered casualty rates near a third of their strength, and neither destroyed the other. Recorded as a Draw rather than a Win: Frederick held the field and the immediate threat to Berlin was checked (hence objective_secured=true), but modern historiography (this dataset follows that reading rather than 18th-century Prussian propaganda declaring outright victory) treats the tactical result itself as inconclusive, and the battered Prussian army could not follow up.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Kunersdorf'
notes: The worst defeat of Frederick's career: a combined Russian-Austrian army under Saltykov (with Laudon's Austrian corps) destroyed roughly 40% of Frederick's field army in a single day; Frederick reportedly carried poison afterward and wrote that he believed all was lost, a collapse only survived because the victors failed to pursue and occupy Berlin. decisiveness is Rout per the schema's definition for a Loss (this general's own army was the one that broke), the only such case in Frederick's roster.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Torgau'
notes: The last great pitched battle of the Seven Years' War for Frederick: a costly frontal-and-flank assault on Daun's fortified position, won only after dark and at a Prussian casualty rate (around 38% of the force engaged) higher than the Austrians suffered. Classed Pyrrhic despite securing Saxony for the winter and forcing Daun's withdrawal, since by this stage of the war Prussia's dwindling manpower (resource_backing_tier=1, matching Zorndorf and Kunersdorf) made a win this costly barely sustainable -- the last two years of the war (1761-1763) settled into attrition and maneuver without another battle of comparable scale.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Montenotte'
notes: Napoleon's first battle as commander-in-chief, splitting the allied Austrian and Sardinian armies and opening the Italian campaign. enemy_casualties (~3,000) includes roughly 2,500-3,500 killed/wounded/captured across sources plus 12 guns lost; figures are small-scale and not heavily contested.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Lodi'
notes: Forced the Adda river crossing against Sebottendorf's Austrian rearguard (the main army under Beaulieu had already withdrawn, so the tactical objective -- the crossing -- was secured, but the strategic opportunity to trap the main Austrian force was missed). enemy_casualties combines ~335 killed/wounded and ~1,700 captured. Tactically minor in scale next to Arcole/Rivoli but reputation-defining for Bonaparte politically ('the little corporal').

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Arcole'
notes: Three days of costly fighting in the Adige marshes against Alvinczi's relief force, breaking the attempt to relieve the besieged fortress of Mantua. Casualty figures vary by source -- some place combined Austrian losses closer to 7,000 rather than the ~6,200 (2,200 killed/wounded + ~4,000 captured) used here.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Rivoli'
notes: Alvinczi's fourth and final attempt to relieve Mantua, destroyed despite the French being outnumbered; roughly half the Austrian force (killed, wounded, or captured) was lost, and Mantua surrendered days later, ending the Italian campaign's main threat. Sources give own_casualties anywhere from 3,200-5,000 and enemy_casualties 12,000-14,300; midpoints used.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of the Pyramids'
notes: Lopsided win over Murad Bey's Mamluk/Ottoman-Egyptian force outside Cairo, secured largely by French infantry-square tactics against Mamluk cavalry. enemy_troop_strength (21,000) is the more conservative widely-cited figure; some sources put the Mamluk/Egyptian force as high as 50,000, a wider disagreement than French strength or casualties (~29 killed, ~260 wounded), which are firmly sourced. Napoleon's Egyptian expedition ultimately failed strategically after Nelson destroyed the supporting fleet at the Nile days later, but that does not bear on this battle's own result.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Marengo'
notes: As First Consul, nearly lost this battle -- Melas's Austrians broke the initial French line and Melas left the field believing he had won, before Desaix's late-arriving division (Desaix was killed in the counterattack) reversed the result. own_casualties disagreement across sources is unusually wide (older figures ~5,600-7,000; modern research, e.g. Boycott-Brown, favors ~9,400); the lower end is used here with the range flagged rather than the newer figure, since it is still the more commonly cited one. Secured French control of northern Italy and led to the Treaty of Luneville.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Austerlitz'
notes: Widely regarded as Napoleon's tactical masterpiece: a deliberately weakened right flank drew the Russo-Austrian army into an attack that let the French cut off and destroy the allied center. opponent_general_id is Kutuzov, the nominal Russian commander-in-chief, though Tsar Alexander I overruled his caution and effectively directed the battle. Broke the Third Coalition and produced the Peace of Pressburg.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Jena-Auerstedt'
notes: This row covers Jena only -- Napoleon's personally-commanded engagement against Hohenlohe's Prussian/Saxon force -- not the simultaneous Battle of Auerstedt fought the same day by Marshal Davout (heavily outnumbered) against the main Prussian army under the Duke of Brunswick, which this dataset excludes as a subordinate-commanded action, the same personal-command bar applied to Genghis Khan's, Saladin's, and Frederick's rosters. Secondary sources frequently conflate the two battles' figures; Jena-specific casualty figures used here (~5,500 French, ~26,500 Prussian/Saxon) are pulled apart from the combined Jena-Auerstedt totals where possible. The two battles together destroyed the Prussian army as a fighting force within a single day.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Friedland'
notes: Decisive win over Bennigsen's Russian army, fought with its back to the Alle river; forced the Treaties of Tilsit. enemy_casualties has an unusually wide spread across sources (roughly 20,000 to 40,000 including captured and drowned in the river crossing); the lower, more conservative modern estimate is used.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Eylau'
notes: A brutally costly, inconclusive winter battle against Bennigsen fought in a blizzard; French held the field at the end but achieved no strategic gain and were forced into defensive winter quarters afterward, so recorded as a Draw rather than a Win despite the nominal field-holding, the same reasoning applied to Frederick's Zorndorf. own_casualties is the single softest figure in this general's roster: French official reports claimed as few as 15,000 while later historians' estimates run close to 29,600, nearly double; the midpoint used here should be read as low-confidence, hence source_confidence=Low rather than this roster's usual Medium.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Wagram'
notes: The largest battle in European history up to that point, fought against Archduke Charles; casualties were nearly even on both sides (French/allied ~35,000 to Austrian ~38,900) and, together with the Peninsular War's ongoing drain, the cost is why this is classed Pyrrhic despite forcing Austria's surrender at the Treaty of Schonbrunn -- the same 'nominal winner, gutting cost' reasoning applied to Frederick's Torgau.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Borodino'
notes: The bloodiest single day of the Napoleonic Wars. Recorded as a Win on the letter of the outcome field (the French held the field at day's end and Kutuzov withdrew), but decisiveness=Pyrrhic and objective_secured=false reflect the strategic reality: the Russian army was battered but escaped intact, Moscow was occupied but abandoned and burning, and the campaign ended in catastrophic retreat -- the single clearest case in this roster of a tactical win with no real strategic payoff. Casualty and strength figures are among the most contested of any battle in this dataset across historians (French strength cited anywhere 103,000-135,000, own_casualties 30,000-42,000, enemy_casualties 40,000-53,000); source_confidence downgraded to Low to reflect that spread rather than this roster's usual Medium.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Leipzig'; World History Encyclopedia 'Battle of Leipzig'
notes: The 'Battle of Nations', the largest battle of the Napoleonic Wars and Napoleon's first major defeat in a set-piece battle, fought against the allied Coalition army under the nominal supreme command of Schwarzenberg (Blucher, Bennigsen, and Bernadotte also commanded major wings). own_casualties (~68,000) combines roughly 38,000 battle casualties with a further ~30,000 troops captured or trapped in the city when the Elster river bridge was blown prematurely during the retreat -- two loss categories combined into one field the way Alesia and the Siege of Acre combine multi-force totals elsewhere in this dataset. Triggered the collapse of French control of Germany and the eventual invasion of France itself.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Waterloo'
notes: Final battle of the Hundred Days. opponent_general_id is Wellington, who held the defended position all day, though the battle's collapse of the French right and the rout that followed were decided by Blucher's Prussian army arriving in the afternoon; enemy_troop_strength (113,000) is the combined Anglo-allied (~68,000) and Prussian (~45,000) total engaged over the course of the day, not just Wellington's initial force. resource_backing_tier=1 reflects Napoleon's isolated, hastily-reconstituted Hundred Days army with no imperial resource base behind it, the lowest of any row in this general's career. Ended Napoleon's rule permanently.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Belmont'
notes: Grant's first battle in independent command: a raid on a Confederate camp across the Mississippi that succeeded tactically but ended in a disorderly Union withdrawal to the transports under counterattack, so it is recorded as a Draw rather than a Win -- the same 'genuinely contested, no clean winner' treatment given to Frederick's Zorndorf and Napoleon's Eylau elsewhere in this dataset. opponent_general_id is Leonidas Polk, the Confederate department commander who dispatched the reinforcements that forced Grant's withdrawal; the immediate counterattacking field commander was Gideon Pillow. own_troop_strength (3,114) is the figure Wikipedia and independent sources agree on; a single search result returned 8,114, which looks like an extraction error against the same underlying page rather than a genuine second estimate.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Fort Henry'; American Battlefield Trust
notes: The fort was reduced primarily by Flag Officer Andrew Foote's ironclad gunboats before Grant's infantry, delayed by rain and mud, arrived to engage; most of the garrison had already withdrawn toward Fort Donelson by the time of surrender. Grant held overall command of the joint army-navy expedition throughout and the resulting capture (opening the Tennessee River, directly enabling the march on Fort Donelson) is credited to him strategically, but this is the one battle on his roster where the land force he personally led saw minimal actual combat -- flagged here rather than excluded, since Grant was present and in command, unlike the subordinate-led battles excluded from other generals' rosters in this dataset. enemy_troop_strength/enemy_casualties are rounded from reported ranges (2,500-3,400 garrison; ~21 combat casualties plus 78-94 captured with the fort).

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Fort Donelson'; American Battlefield Trust
notes: The 'unconditional surrender' battle that made Grant's national reputation. enemy_casualties (13,846) is overwhelmingly the roughly 12,392 Confederate troops captured en masse rather than battle deaths, effectively destroying the garrison as a fighting force -- hence Rout. opponent_general_id is Simon Bolivar Buckner, who actually negotiated and executed the surrender with Grant; nominal senior commanders John B. Floyd and Gideon Pillow fled by boat and on foot the night before rather than surrender personally. Wikipedia and American Battlefield Trust figures match exactly.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Shiloh'; American Battlefield Trust
notes: own_troop_strength/own_casualties are the combined Army of the Tennessee (Grant, roughly 44,000-49,000 engaged) plus Army of the Ohio (Buell, ~17,918, arrived the night of day one and fought under Buell's own independent command, not subordinate to Grant) totals as conventionally reported for 'the Battle of Shiloh' -- Grant was senior officer present and directed the decisive day-two counterattack, but a real share of the force and casualties were not under his direct command, a comparable complication to how Napoleon's Waterloo row combines Wellington's and Blucher's forces. opponent_general_id is Albert Sidney Johnston, who planned and led the Confederate attack and was killed in action on day one; P.G.T. Beauregard commanded the Confederate army for day two. The battle's then-unprecedented cost (~24,000 combined casualties) triggered a political firestorm and calls for Grant's removal that Lincoln overrode ('I can't spare this man; he fights') -- political_constraint_flag=true reflects the sustained pressure this placed on Grant's command through mid-1862.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Champion Hill'; American Battlefield Trust
notes: own_troop_strength has a real cross-source disagreement (Wikipedia's 32,000 vs. American Battlefield Trust's 54,000); 32,000, the force actually engaged on the field that day, is used here since McClernand's corps was slow to arrive and only partially committed, while 54,000 appears to reflect total Union manpower available in the campaign area rather than troops fighting at Champion Hill specifically -- confidence downgraded to Medium for this field alone (casualty figures agree exactly across sources). Loring's Confederate division was cut off from the battlefield and never rejoined Pemberton's army, effectively lost to the campaign even though the main Confederate force survived to retreat into Vicksburg, which is why this is coded Strategic rather than Rout.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Siege of Vicksburg'; American Battlefield Trust
notes: own_troop_strength shows the same Wikipedia (~77,000) vs. ABT (110,000) split seen at Champion Hill and Chattanooga in this campaign/theater; 75,000, the besieging force actually deployed around Vicksburg, is used rather than ABT's apparent total-department figure, confidence downgraded to Medium for this field. enemy_casualties (32,697) is almost entirely the roughly 29,500 Confederate garrison surrendered outright on July 4 rather than battle deaths -- an entire Confederate field army destroyed as a fighting force, hence Rout. Secured the Mississippi River and split the Confederacy, the stated Union strategic objective of the whole Western Theater campaign, and Grant's most unambiguously personal campaign of the war (47 days in continuous personal command).

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Chattanooga campaign'; American Battlefield Trust
notes: own_troop_strength (72,533) is the force actually concentrated for the Nov 23-25 fighting, not ABT's 121,400 figure for Grant's entire Military Division of the Mississippi across all posts -- the same theater-total-vs-engaged-force pattern seen at Champion Hill and Vicksburg in this roster. enemy_casualties is a genuine range (6,000-8,684) reflecting Bragg's incomplete post-rout reporting; 7,000 is used as a rounded midpoint. The decisive moment, Thomas's troops storming past their ordered objective (the rifle pits at the base of Missionary Ridge) all the way to the crest, was spontaneous soldier/subordinate initiative beyond Grant's or Thomas's actual orders -- Grant set the overall campaign plan and is credited with the victory, but the specific tactical breakthrough was not his direct order, worth noting given the personal-command bar applied elsewhere in this dataset.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of the Wilderness'; American Battlefield Trust
notes: Recorded as a Draw per both sources' 'inconclusive' characterization -- neither army broke, and Grant disengaged to continue the march south rather than retreating, which is the battle's real historical significance (previous Union commanders in Virginia had withdrawn after a bloody repulse; Grant did not). objective_secured=false reflects that Lee's army was neither defeated nor dislodged tactically. Command complication shared with Spotsylvania, Cold Harbor, and the Petersburg assaults below: Grant, as general-in-chief, traveled with the Army of the Potomac and directed overall strategy, while George Meade remained the army's formal commander issuing tactical orders -- historians (e.g. Gordon Rhea) generally credit Grant for strategic direction and Meade for tactical execution; treated here as Grant's battle on the strategic-direction standard, the same 'personally supreme-commanded' bar used for Genghis Khan and Saladin elsewhere in this dataset. political_constraint_flag=true reflects the well-documented pressure of the looming 1864 election, which shaped Grant's decision to keep pressing south after this and the following Overland Campaign battles rather than withdraw.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Spotsylvania Court House'; American Battlefield Trust
notes: Troop-strength figures for both sides carry the largest cross-source disagreement in this general's roster: Wikipedia's 108,000-115,400 Union / 52,000-63,000 Confederate versus ABT's 152,000 / 100,000, a spread of 40,000+ on each side, most likely explained by ABT citing total army effective strength rather than troops actually engaged in the Spotsylvania fighting specifically -- source_confidence downgraded to Low for this field, distinct from the otherwise exact agreement on casualties across sources. Same Grant/Meade shared-command note as the Wilderness applies. Two weeks of near-continuous fighting (including the 'Bloody Angle' at the Mule Shoe salient) ended with Lee's lines intact and Grant again sidestepping south rather than retreating -- coded Draw/objective_secured=false on the same tactical-inconclusive standard as the Wilderness.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Cold Harbor'; American Battlefield Trust
notes: The clearest Loss in Grant's Civil War record -- Wikipedia's infobox states a Confederate victory outright, and Grant himself later wrote in his memoirs that he regretted ordering the June 3 frontal assault, which gained 'no advantage whatever ... to compensate for the heavy loss.' Troop strengths again show the large Wikipedia-vs-ABT spread (55,000+ on each side) seen at Spotsylvania, downgrading source_confidence to Low for that field; own_casualties (12,738) agrees closely across sources, but enemy_casualties is subject to genuine historian debate -- Gordon Rhea has specifically argued the popular narrative of '7,000 Union casualties in 20 minutes' on June 3 overstates the case, with reconstructed Confederate losses across the full multi-day battle closer to the ~5,000-5,300 range used here. Unlike the Wilderness/Spotsylvania's shared Grant/Meade command framing, this assault is the one Overland Campaign battle Grant personally and explicitly took responsibility for.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Second Battle of Petersburg'
notes: The opening assaults of what became the Siege of Petersburg: repeated Union attacks against Beauregard's thin defending garrison over four days were repulsed, forcing the shift from open assault to formal siege warfare -- hence Loss/objective_secured=false despite the campaign's eventual success ten months later. Troop strength is reported as a wide range on both sides (Union 13,700-62,000; Confederate 5,400-38,000) reflecting heavy reinforcement over the four days as more of the Army of the Potomac and Lee's army arrived; the upper/peak figures are used here, confidence downgraded to Low for that field. Treated as one row of a four-row breakdown of the 9.5-month Siege of Petersburg (with the Battle of the Crater, Battle of Globe Tavern, and the Third Battle of Petersburg below) rather than one aggregate siege-level row, since the siege's distinct, separately-documented actions had genuinely different outcomes and are better served by the same per-named-battle granularity used throughout this dataset. opponent_general_id is P.G.T. Beauregard, who commanded the thin defending garrison before Lee's main army arrived from the Overland Campaign; Lee took over direct command only as the assaults were ending.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of the Crater'
notes: A mine packed with four tons of gunpowder was detonated under the Confederate lines, but the follow-up Union assault collapsed into the resulting crater and was destroyed there by a Confederate counterattack (led on the ground by William Mahone, under Lee's overall command) -- Grant himself called it 'the saddest affair I have witnessed in the war.' The disaster is attributed principally to subordinate command failures (Burnside's planning, Ledlie's absent leadership of the lead division) rather than to any direct tactical order from Grant, though it happened under his and Meade's overall direction of the siege. Troop-strength and casualty figures agree closely across sources.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Globe Tavern'
notes: Union forces permanently cut the Weldon Railroad, one of Petersburg and Richmond's last supply lines, a genuine strategic gain despite Union casualties (4,296, mostly captured when a division was surprised and overrun on the first day) running more than double Confederate losses (1,620) -- decisiveness=Strategic rather than Tactical since the railroad stayed cut for the rest of the siege. opponent_general_id is A.P. Hill, who led the Confederate counterattacks, under Lee's overall command of the siege lines.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Third Battle of Petersburg'
notes: The breakthrough that actually ended the nearly ten-month Siege of Petersburg: Union forces finally broke through Lee's thinned defensive lines, killing Confederate corps commander A.P. Hill and forcing the evacuation of Petersburg and Richmond the next day, which triggered the week-long pursuit ending at Appomattox. Troop strengths given as troops actually engaged (63,000 Union of 114,335 total; 18,000-20,000 Confederate of 40,000-45,000 total, most of the depleted Army of Northern Virginia not directly engaged in this specific assault) rather than full army totals, confidence Medium for that field. political_constraint_flag=false: with Lincoln already re-elected in November 1864, the acute 1864 campaign-season political pressure noted on the Overland Campaign and earlier Petersburg rows no longer applied. Coded Strategic rather than Rout since Lee's army, though broken here, retreated in some order toward Appomattox rather than disintegrating on the field.

source_citation: Wikipedia 'Battle of Appomattox Court House'; American Battlefield Trust
notes: Final battle of the war in Virginia: Lee's remaining army, surrounded and out of options, surrendered after brief final skirmishing. Grant personally directed the closing pursuit and personally negotiated the surrender terms with Lee -- the least ambiguous 'Grant's battle' of the whole war for personal command and historical association. own_casualties is Wikipedia's 164 killed-or-wounded figure; ABT gives a slightly different breakdown (152: 14 killed, 74 wounded, 64 missing/captured), a minor discrepancy given how light this battle was. enemy_casualties (26,500) combines the day's roughly 500 combat casualties (195 killed, 305 wounded) with the approximately 26,000 troops surrendered, following the same 'surrendered-army-as-casualties' convention used for Vicksburg and Fort Donelson elsewhere in this dataset -- sources vary 26,000-28,356 depending on whether non-combatant personnel present at the surrender are counted.
